editorial:
According to Wikipedia, International Crime (released 22 April 1938) is a 62-minute Grand National Pictures mystery directed by Charles Lamont. Rod La Rocque plays Lamont Cranston, who operates as The Shadow, and Astrid Allwyn, Thomas E. Jackson and William Pawley play opposite him. Wikipedia credits the story 'Foxhound' to Theodore A. Tinsley and the screenplay to Jack Natteford. A creator might want it as a pulp-era Shadow feature with a newspaper setting and a spy plot.

The film's copyright status is not settled. My text search of the Catalog of Copyright Entries OCR for 1965-1967 found no renewal, but it covered only part of each volume, so it does not prove that none exists. Check the volumes by hand before treating the film as public domain. The character and the source story are separate questions. The Shadow is a long-lived franchise, and I did not check whether the 'Foxhound' story or any Shadow trademark is still held by someone. The music is also unchecked. Do not market a new work as an official Shadow property without clearing the character.
faq: Is the 1938 International Crime film itself still under copyright?

Not confirmed either way. A text search of the archive.org OCR of the 1965, 1966 and 1967 Catalog of Copyright Entries motion-picture volumes found no renewal, but the fetch covered only part of each volume. A renewal could also be filed under another title or claimant name, or be missed by OCR. Check the volumes by hand before relying on public-domain status.
Can I make new Shadow stories or use the Shadow name with this footage?

The footage is one thing and the character is another. I did not verify the status of the source story or of any Shadow trademark. Using the film unchanged is a different matter from calling a new work 'The Shadow', and that second use needs separate clearance.
